title: How Spiritual Warfare ACTUALLY Works (w/ Darius J Wright)
summary: Darius J Wright, drawing on his out-of-body experiences, describes spiritual warfare as a contest between thought-form spirits of love and of fear, with hell as a temporary state of separation from love and unconditional love as the force that lifts the fallen back. The hosts tie this to their reading of the first Nazarene Christians as opposed to animal sacrifice and practicing baptism in its place, while the second half moves into claims about elite blood rituals, vaccines, adrenochrome, NASA and water memory.

topics.title: HELL AS THE ABSENCE OF LOVE
topics.lead: Darius and the hosts argue that hell is real but not permanent: a state of separation from love whose depth matches how far a soul has stepped out of love.

claims.phrase: the unforgivable sin is a sin you can't forgive yourself for
claims.speaker: Darius J Wright
claims.claim: The unforgivable sin is a sin a person cannot forgive themselves for.
claims.check: In the gospels, the sin that "shall not be forgiven" is blasphemy against the Holy Ghost (Matthew 12:31-32), set against speaking a word against the Son of man, which can be forgiven. The mainstream reading takes it as a hardened, deliberate rejection of God's Spirit. Reading it as self-unforgiveness is a psychological interpretation; the text doesn't say it.

claims.phrase: Not that you will be in that realm forever, but in the spiritual realm,
claims.speaker: Aaron
claims.claim: When Jesus speaks of "everlasting fire" he means the realm of fire is eternal, not that a person stays there forever.
claims.check: Matthew 25:41 does apply aionios ("everlasting") to the fire, "prepared for the devil and his angels", which leaves room for this reading. But 25:46 applies the same word to the punishment itself ("everlasting punishment") in parallel with "life eternal", which is the strongest verse against it. Aionios can mean "of the age" as well as "without end"; scholars and traditions still disagree.

sources.title: Strong's Greek 166: aiónios (Bible Hub), Thayer's entry
sources.quote: without end, never to cease, everlasting

claims.phrase: You will go to where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth.
claims.speaker: Aaron
claims.claim: Jesus warns that people who do not do good works go where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth.
claims.check: The phrase is Jesus's own and recurs in Matthew (8:12; 22:13; 25:30; 13:42 has "wailing and gnashing"). At 25:30 it closes the parable of the talents, where the servant is cast out for doing nothing with what he was given, so tying it to conduct fits the text.

claims.phrase: I I believe he talks about 10 or 12.
claims.speaker: Darius J Wright
claims.claim: The Bible speaks of three or seven heavens, and the book of Enoch of ten or twelve.
claims.check: The only numbered heaven in the KJV is Paul's "third heaven" (2 Corinthians 12:2); seven heavens are not counted anywhere in the Bible. A ten-heaven scheme appears in 2 Enoch (Slavonic Enoch), not 1 Enoch, and scholars think it was expanded from seven by a later editor. No ancient source found gives twelve heavens.

sources.title: 2 Enoch, Early Jewish Writings (Rost)
sources.quote: Enoch's journey through the ten heavens (originally perhaps only seven heavens)

topics.title: SACRIFICE AND THE FIRST NAZARENES
topics.lead: The hosts argue that Jesus's first followers were Torah-observant Jews who called themselves Nazarenes and rejected animal sacrifice and meat, and Darius links sacrifice to the worship of Moloch.

claims.phrase: And Nazarenes is the northern sect of Essenes in the 1st century.
claims.speaker: unclear
claims.claim: The Nazarenes were the northern sect of the Essenes in the first century, and Jesus emerged from that sect.
claims.check: Acts 24:5 does call the movement "the sect of the Nazarenes". Epiphanius (Panarion 18) also describes a separate group, the Nasaraeans, Jews from Gilead, Bashan and Transjordan who would not sacrifice or eat meat, and keeps them distinct from the Christian Nazoraeans (Panarion 29). Treating Nasaraeans and Ossaeans as the two Essene branches is J. B. Lightfoot's 19th-century reading. No ancient source calls Jesus's Nazarenes a sect of the Essenes.

sources.title: Nazarene (sect), Wikipedia
sources.quote: they were Jews who kept all the Jewish observances, but they would not offer sacrifice or eat meat.

sources.title: Nazarene (sect), Wikipedia
sources.quote: Epiphanius also makes a distinction between the Ossaeans and the Nasaraeans,

claims.phrase: or the second person of the Trinity. These ideas came hundreds of years later.
claims.speaker: unclear
claims.claim: The ideas that Jesus was God incarnate or the second person of the Trinity came hundreds of years later.
claims.check: The Trinity as a formal doctrine was settled at Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381), and the word trinitas first appears with Tertullian around 213. But very high claims about Jesus are already in first-century texts: John 1:1 and the apostle Thomas's "My LORD and my God" (John 20:28). What came later was the creedal formula, not every exalted claim.

claims.phrase: all these sources unanimously agree with one another that the first Christians, the Nazarenes,
claims.speaker: unclear
claims.claim: The Clementine writings, the Didache, the Hebrew Gospel of Matthew and other Nazarene sources all agree that the first Christians opposed animal sacrifice.
claims.check: The Clementine Recognitions say so plainly: Moses allowed sacrifice for a time (1.36), and the true Prophet was to end it (1.37). The Didache doesn't: it bans food offered to idols but on food otherwise says "undertake what you can" (6:3), and it calls the community's own Eucharist a "sacrifice" (14). The Qumran texts prescribe sacrifice. So the claim holds for the Clementine stream, not for every early source.

sources.title: Clementine Recognitions, Book I (New Advent, ANF vol. 8)
sources.quote: he allowed them indeed to sacrifice, but permitted it to be done only to God

claims.phrase: the eating and consumption of animal flesh is as polluting as the worship of demons.
claims.speaker: unclear
claims.claim: These sources teach that eating animal flesh pollutes as much as worshipping demons.
claims.check: In the Clementine Homilies, Peter lists "to abstain from the table of devils, not to taste dead flesh, not to touch blood" together (Homilies 7.4). The law given to the demons says they rule over people who share their table or are "tasting dead flesh" (8.19). That fits the claim for the Clementine Homilies specifically; the Didache, as noted above, does not say this.

claims.phrase: that Moses never commanded these abominations like the prophets have said, right? Jeremiah, Isaiah.
claims.speaker: unclear
claims.claim: The prophets Jeremiah and Isaiah said Moses never commanded animal sacrifice.
claims.check: Jeremiah 7:22 says it in God's voice: "I spake not unto your fathers, nor commanded them... concerning burnt offerings or sacrifices." Isaiah 1:11 rejects the sacrifices ("I delight not in the blood of bullocks") but doesn't say Moses never commanded them. Against both stand Leviticus 1:2 and Jeremiah 33:18, which promises priests "to do sacrifice continually". Whether 7:22 is a flat denial or a statement of priorities is still argued.

topics.title: BAPTISM AND THE MEMORY OF WATER
topics.lead: The hosts present baptism as the Essene and Nazarene replacement for animal sacrifice and claim that water can be restructured by speech, then read Pentecost as a group out-of-body experience.

claims.phrase: they they did baptism as a righteous substitute for the animal sacrifice.
claims.speaker: unclear
claims.claim: The Essenes and Nazarenes practiced baptism as a righteous substitute for animal sacrifice, and did it daily as a recommitment.
claims.check: Clementine Recognitions 1.39 says nearly this: the Prophet "instituted baptism by water" so that people would be purified "not by the blood of beasts". For the Essenes it is shakier. Josephus says they kept away from the Temple sacrifices because they had "more pure lustrations of their own" (Ant. 18.1.5), but the repo flags that sentence as textually uncertain, and Qumran texts prescribe sacrifice. Daily washings are attested (Peter bathes each morning in Homilies 10-11), but they are ritual baths, not a repeated baptism.

sources.title: Clementine Recognitions, Book I, ch. 39 (New Advent, ANF vol. 8)
sources.quote: being purified not by the blood of beasts, but by the purification of the Wisdom of God

claims.phrase: it has been absolutely proven scientifically through the work of people like Veda Austin.
claims.speaker: unclear
claims.claim: It is scientifically proven that speaking words over water changes how it crystallizes (Veda Austin, Masaru Emoto).
claims.check: Emoto's water-crystal work isn't accepted science. Critics point to weak controls and designs that let the photographer pick which crystals to show, and his one co-authored paper appeared in a fringe journal. No independent, controlled replication shows that words change water's structure. Veda Austin's crystallography has not been published in peer-reviewed science either.

sources.title: Masaru Emoto, Wikipedia
sources.quote: hard to see how anyone could mistake it for science.

sources.title: Masaru Emoto, Wikipedia
sources.quote: It is very unlikely that there is any reality behind Emoto's claims.

claims.phrase: they all heard the sound as of a rushing mighty river.
claims.speaker: Aaron
claims.claim: Acts 2 describes a sound like a rushing mighty river and tongues of fire over the disciples' heads, which matches the onset of an out-of-body experience.
claims.check: The text says wind, not river: "a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind" (Acts 2:2), and "cloven tongues like as of fire" sat upon each of them (2:3). Reading Pentecost as a group out-of-body experience is Aaron's interpretation from his own experience. Acts presents it as the coming of the Holy Spirit.

topics.title: SCRIPTURE QUOTED ON THE FLY
topics.lead: Several verses are quoted from memory during the conversation; some are accurate, some are misattributed or misremembered.

claims.phrase: And the Greek word for um kill is thuo, which literally means animal sacrifice.
claims.speaker: unclear
claims.claim: In John 10:10 the devil comes to kill, steal and destroy, and the Greek word for kill, thuo, literally means animal sacrifice.
claims.check: The verse is John 10:10, not John 5, and its subject is "the thief", not the devil. Thuo does mean to sacrifice, but it also means simply to slaughter or kill for food: the fatted calf (Luke 15:23) and Peter's "kill, and eat" (Acts 10:13) use it. Thayer's lexicon files John 10:10 under "to slaughter". A sacrificial overtone is possible but not the literal meaning.

sources.title: Strong's Greek 2380: thuó (Bible Hub)
sources.quote: thuó: To sacrifice, to slay, to kill

sources.title: Strong's Greek 2380: thuó (Bible Hub), Thayer's entry

claims.phrase: I think Jesus said, "Resist the devil and he will flee from you."
claims.speaker: unclear
claims.claim: Jesus said, "Resist the devil and he will flee from you."
claims.check: These are the words of the Letter of James, not Jesus: "Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you" (James 4:7). Fittingly, that's James the Just's letter in tradition, but it isn't red text.

claims.phrase: I believe the the literal Greek translation would be kingdom of God come,
claims.speaker: unclear
claims.claim: The literal Greek of the Lord's Prayer reads "kingdom of God come, will of God be done".
claims.check: The Greek of Matthew 6:10 says "your kingdom", not "kingdom of God": elthato he basileia sou, literally "let come the kingdom of you". In context "your" means the Father, so the meaning is the same. But the claim about the literal wording is wrong. The KJV reads "Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven."

claims.phrase: there's something in the scriptures that say do not alter your DNA.
claims.speaker: Darius J Wright
claims.claim: Scripture says not to alter your DNA, or "do not corrupt what God has made".
claims.check: No verse says this. The nearest text is Deuteronomy 4:16, "Lest ye corrupt yourselves, and make you a graven image", which is about idols, and Aaron's first guess on air was the graven-image command. Genesis 1:31 ("every thing that he had made... was very good") is the closest idea, but it isn't a command.

topics.title: THE CONSPIRACY CLAIMS, CHECKED
topics.lead: Darius describes elite blood rituals, harmful vaccines, harvested child tissue and NASA secrets as the physical side of spiritual warfare; these are the checkable claims.

claims.phrase: someone that works for NASA use that on his on his death his his tombstone?
claims.speaker: Darius J Wright
claims.claim: Wernher von Braun, a NASA rocket scientist, has Psalm 19:1 on his gravestone.
claims.check: The fact holds: von Braun is buried at Ivy Hill Cemetery and his gravestone cites Psalm 19:1, "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork." He was also, as said on air, a former Nazi Party and SS member who led NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center. The "mocking" reading is speculation. A plainer explanation is that he became an evangelical Christian later in life.

sources.title: Wernher von Braun, Wikipedia
sources.quote: Shortly after, he converted to Evangelicalism.

claims.phrase: You You stick a vaccine in there. Some of these are baby parts, fetus, foreskin.
claims.speaker: Darius J Wright
claims.claim: Vaccines contain baby parts, fetal tissue, foreskin and heavy metals, and are designed to alter your DNA.
claims.check: Some vaccines (chickenpox, rubella, hepatitis A, one rabies vaccine) are grown in cell lines first taken from two elective abortions in the 1960s. No new fetal tissue is used, and the vaccines contain no fetal cells, only possible traces of fragmented DNA or protein. mRNA vaccines do not enter the cell nucleus and cannot change a person's DNA.

sources.title: Vaccine Ingredients: Fetal Tissues, Children's Hospital of Philadelphia Vaccine Education Center
sources.quote: No further sources of fetal cells are needed to make these vaccines.

sources.title: Claims that mRNA vaccines change human DNA are back, Washington University Health Communication Research Lab
sources.quote: mRNA only enters the cell cytoplasm and does not enter the cell's nucleus where human DNA is found.

claims.phrase: Actually taking baby flesh body parts into what what we consume.
claims.speaker: Darius J Wright
claims.claim: Aborted babies' body parts are sold on black markets and put into products and food that people consume.
claims.check: This has been checked repeatedly and found false. The usual source is the HEK-293 cell line, cloned from fetal kidney tissue in the early 1970s and used in labs to mimic taste receptors when testing flavourings. The cells are not in the food, and major food companies confirmed they don't use flavourings developed with them.

sources.title: There aren't human foetal cells in lots of popular snacks and drinks, Full Fact
sources.quote: HEK-293 is not in the flavouring itself.

claims.phrase: from young youth, purity, innocence, it helps sustain your life.
claims.speaker: Darius J Wright
claims.claim: Adrenochrome is real, and drinking adrenaline-rich blood from young victims helps sustain life.
claims.check: Only the narrow part holds: adrenochrome is a real compound formed when adrenaline oxidizes. It has been made by ordinary chemical synthesis since at least 1952, so nobody would need to harvest it, and no evidence shows it extends life or restores youth. The harvested-from-children story is a modern conspiracy theory, not a documented practice.

sources.title: Adrenochrome, Wikipedia

questions: What does aionios mean in Matthew 25:41 and 25:46: "eternal" or "belonging to the age"? How do annihilationist, universalist and traditional readers each handle 25:46?

Clementine Recognitions 1.36-39 ties the end of sacrifice to baptism. How does that compare with John the Baptist's baptism "for the remission of sins" and with Qumran's warning that washing without inner change purifies nothing (1QS 3:4-7)?
Were Epiphanius's pre-Christian Nasaraeans connected to Jesus's Nazoraeans, or only similar in name? What did Lightfoot base his Essene grouping on?
Why does the Didache say about food "undertake what you can" and ban only idol meat, while the Clementine Homilies treat dead flesh as the demons' table?
What do near-death experience researchers actually report about distressing or hellish experiences, and how often, as against the reports of light and love?
corrections: "Resist the devil and he will flee from you" is James 4:7, not a saying of Jesus.

The thief who comes "to steal, and to kill, and to destroy" is John 10:10 (not John 5), and the subject is "the thief", not the devil. Thuo also means plain slaughter (Luke 15:23; Acts 10:13), so it doesn't "literally mean animal sacrifice" every time.
Acts 2:2 has "a rushing mighty wind", not a river.

Ezekiel 1:16 describes "a wheel in the middle of a wheel" beside the living creatures, not stars or a "ring within rings". Seraphim appear in Isaiah 6:2, not Ezekiel. Hubble's MyCn18 image is the Hourglass Nebula, which ESA/Hubble describes as "a young planetary nebula located about 8,000 light-years away".

NASA did not buy Nikon or discontinue its zoom cameras. The P900 was discontinued, but Nikon's superzoom line went on: the P1000 came out in 2018, and Nikon announced the P1100 as its replacement in 2025.

"Spirit Cooking" is a 1996 artwork by Marina Abramović, cookbook-style instructions painted in pig's blood. The 2015 email that started the story invited Tony Podesta (John's brother) to a dinner. There is no evidence of blood sacrifice, and Hillary Clinton was not part of it.
Skincare products said to contain "foreskin" use growth factors from fibroblasts grown in labs from donated newborn foreskin cells. The Steve Harvey segment described on air could not be verified.
Jeremiah 7:22 does deny that God commanded sacrifice at the Exodus, but don't present it as the prophets' unanimous view without Jeremiah 33:18 and Leviticus 1:2 beside it.
